summary: RFC 8519 defines a YANG data model for access control lists. This document adds augmentations that fix many limitations of that model and extend what it can describe.

eli5.summary: A bouncer's guest list needs room for more details. This upgrades the standard format for those lists so they can express more rules.

subtitle: New YANG building blocks that let router ACLs use shared lists, richer matches and more actions than the original model allowed.

tldr.problem: The ACL data model from RFC 8519 cannot hold lists of prefixes or ports, handles IPv4 fragments and TCP flags poorly, has no IPv6 fragment, payload or MPLS matching, and offers no rate-limit action.
tldr.mechanism: A new YANG module, ietf-acl-enh, augments the RFC 8519 model with reusable named defined sets, extra match fields (fragments, TCP flag bitmasks, payload patterns, MPLS, VLAN, I-SID) and extra actions (rate-limit, log, counter).
tldr.outcome: Operators can express large filtering policies with far fewer rules and manage the sets separately from the rules. The document also creates three IANA-maintained YANG modules for ICMPv4 types, ICMPv6 types and IPv6 extension header types.

facts.label: Defined-set kinds
facts.value: IPv4 prefix, IPv6 prefix, port, protocol, ICMPv4 type, ICMPv6 type, alias

today: RFC 9899 is a Standards Track document with Proposed Standard status, published in December 2025. It augments the model of RFC 8519, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Original ACL Model Falls Short
sections.content:
RFC 8519 defines Access Control Lists (ACLs) in YANG as a user-ordered set of filtering rules, each called an Access Control Entry (ACE). RFC 9899 identifies a set of limitations in that model and fixes them with augmentations, which are additions layered on top of the base model rather than changes to it.

The main motivation is scale and manageability. Matching against 100 IP addresses should take a single rule, not 100 ACEs. If the rule refers to a named list instead of literal addresses, an operator can add or remove entries without rewriting the rule. ACLs and sets can also be defined at the network or administrative-domain level and then associated with several devices, instead of being tied to one device as in RFC 8519.

The document also notes that ACLs are used locally on devices but are often triggered by other tools such as DDoS mitigation (RFC 9132) or BGP Flow Spec (RFC 8955, RFC 8956), so it helps if the model maps easily to the filtering rules those tools carry. The module conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). Appendix A holds the full gap analysis.
sections.eli5: The old guest-list format made you write every name out one by one. This new version lets you point to a group and change the group whenever you like.

sections.title: How the Enhanced Module Is Built
sections.content:
The module is named ietf-acl-enh. It imports types from the RFC 8519 ACL modules and adds nodes in several places in the ACL tree: a defined-sets container directly under acls, new fields under an ACE's matches (payload, alias and MPLS choices, plus Layer 2, IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP additions), and new nodes under actions.

Much of the work is done by reusable YANG groupings such as tcp-flags, fragment-fields, mpls-match-parameters-config, payload-match and acl-complementary-actions. Optional behaviour is gated by YANG features, for example match-on-payload, match-on-vlan-filter, match-on-isid-filter, match-on-alias and match-on-mpls, so a device can implement only the parts it supports.

The first revision of the module is dated 2025-12-22.
sections.eli5: Think of a toy set with the basic bricks already in the box. This document adds new bricks that snap onto the old ones, and you only use the bricks your toy needs.

sections.title: Defined Sets and Aliases
sections.content:
A defined set is a named collection of elements that share a purpose, such as IP addresses, IP prefixes, port numbers or ICMP types. Each set has a unique name, and an ACE refers to it by name. The module defines these kinds:

  • IPv4 and IPv6 prefix sets: a match succeeds if the source or destination address falls within any prefix in the set.
  • Port sets: port numbers for TCP and UDP entries. Each entry is a range or a single port with an operator (equal to, greater than or equal to, and so on).
  • Protocol sets: protocols given by number (for example 17) or by name (for example UDP).
  • ICMP sets: ICMPv4 or ICMPv6 types, each optionally refined by code and rest of header.
  • Aliases: a combination of parameters such as prefix, protocol, port, VLAN, FQDN or URI. The RFC says to use a plain set when only one parameter is involved.

The RFC's alias example is a group of HTTPS servers: their two IPv6 addresses together with TCP port 443. Sets and aliases can be defined at the network level and then reused across devices.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing 'Ann, Bo, Cy' on every note, you name the group 'the book club' once and just say 'the book club' wherever you need it.

sections.title: New Match Fields and Actions
sections.content:
Beyond sets, the module adds several new ways to match a packet:

  • TCP flags: a flags-bitmask container with an operator and either explicit flag identities or a numeric bitmask. A client that supports both flags-bitmask and the RFC 8519 flags field MUST NOT set both in the same request.
  • Fragments: ipv4-fragment and ipv6-fragment take an operator and a fragment type: df (don't fragment, which must be 0 in an IPv6 filter), isf (is a fragment), ff (first fragment) or lf (last fragment).
  • IPv6 extension headers: an extension-header leaf typed by a new IANA-maintained module.
  • Payload patterns: under the match-on-payload feature, a data offset, a length and a binary pattern are compared using an operator. The offset type can start at Layer 2, Layer 3, Layer 4 or the transport payload. The RFC suggests uses such as QUIC and tunneling protocols.
  • MPLS: traffic class, label position (top or bottom), upper and lower label range, label block name and TTL value.
  • VLAN and I-SID: a range (lower and upper) or an operator with a list of values. An I-SID is the 24-bit Instance Service Identifier used by Provider Backbone Bridging.

The operator type is a set of bits. not negates, match means (data & value) == value, and any means (data & value) != 0. The any and match bits must not be set together.

For actions, RFC 8519 only offers accept, drop and reject. This module adds rate-limit, a decimal64 value with two fraction digits in bytes per second that is valid only when the forwarding action is accept. It also adds log-action and counter-action. This version supports only local actions.
sections.eli5: The bouncer can now check more things, like a hand stamp or how fast people are arriving. He can also say 'you may enter, but only a few at a time' or write down who came in.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix B gives JSON request bodies for the new features. Three show the style:

  • TCP null attack: a flags-bitmask with operator not any and bitmask 4095 drops TCP messages that have no flags set.
  • DNS with fragments dropped: an ACL with two ACEs in order. The first, drop-all-fragments, drops packets matched by isf. The second, allow-dns-packets, accepts UDP destination port 53 to 198.51.100.0/24. The IPv6 variant does the same for 2001:db8::/32 and drops packets that include a Fragment header (44), including atomic fragments.
  • SYN flood: an ACE matches TCP flags with operator match and bitmask 2, uses forwarding accept, and sets rate-limit to 20.00.

The appendix also has examples for pattern-based, VLAN and I-SID filtering.
sections.eli5: The examples are like sample recipes: one says 'turn away anyone with no ticket', and another says 'let guests in but only a few per minute'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040). Those protocols have to use a secure transport and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The defined-sets subtree is called out as sensitive. Unauthorized writes could let an intruder change entries to permit traffic that should be denied, or deny traffic that should be permitted. The sets are tagged nacm:default-deny-write. Unauthorized reads would reveal which resources are bound to ACLs, which helps an attacker target a specific network and can defeat topology-hiding strategies, for example by exposing core router addresses.

For payload pattern matching, the RFC says filtering is deterministic for unencrypted data, but for encrypted packets its efficiency depends on an unvarying pattern being present. The three IANA-maintained modules only define types, expose no writable or state data nodes, and add no extra security issues.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could edit the guest list, they could sneak in or lock out your friends. So only trusted people may change it, and even looking at it should be limited.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Modules
sections.content:
IANA registered four XML namespace URIs and four YANG module names: ietf-acl-enh (prefix acl-enh, not maintained by IANA) and three modules maintained by IANA: iana-icmpv4-types, iana-icmpv6-types and iana-ipv6-ext-types.

This document creates the initial version of each IANA-maintained module. For ICMPv4, IANA added a note that new values must not be added directly to the YANG module but to the 'ICMP Type Numbers' registry. When a value is added to that registry, a new enum is added to the module. The enum name replicates the registry name with illegal characters such as spaces stripped, and value holds the decimal value. The latest module versions are retrieved from the 'YANG Parameters' registry group.
sections.eli5: Some lists, like the official list of ICMP message types, are kept by a librarian called IANA. The computer-readable versions are now updated by the librarian whenever the main list changes.
